claims.text: The unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is nanocrystalline.
Cr-V-rich precipitates begin to form in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 near 8 dpa.
The unmodified alloy exhibits increased irradiation-induced hardening near 8 dpa.
Adding approximately 3–5 at% Hf will produce a uniform Hf distribution in the nanocrystalline BCC matrix.
Uniformly dispersed Hf atoms introduce local lattice distortion.
Hf-induced lattice distortion acts as a barrier to Cr diffusion.
Hf-induced lattice distortion acts as a barrier to V diffusion.
A 3–5 at% Hf addition increases lattice strain and solid-solution strengthening.
Reduced Cr and V diffusivity limits their irradiation-induced clustering.
Limiting Cr and V clustering inhibits nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich precipitates.
The Hf addition will significantly reduce or completely suppress Cr-V-rich precipitates relative to unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation-induced hardening.
The Hf-modified alloy will have radiation resistance comparable to or better than unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The precipitate-suppression mechanism will operate through irradiation doses up to 8 dpa.
The precipitate-suppression mechanism will operate at specimen temperatures of 300–400 °C.
The Hf addition will not require a change to the overall alloy-processing or bulk-fabrication techniques.
The unmodified alloy's precipitate formation around 8 dpa is associated with increased hardness.
The unmodified alloy's precipitate formation around 8 dpa is associated with increased brittleness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome describe the intervention as preserving negligible or low irradiation-induced hardening, which implies a low-hardening baseline, whereas the material-initial-state and baseline fields state that unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 has increased hardening near 8 dpa.
